title: 英伟达股东注意！这家AI巨头的IPO，可能拖累整个板块

keyPoints.text: DeepSeek previously triggered massive market panic around Nvidia, causing its stock to fall from around $130-$150 to roughly $80 over concerns that training top models requires far fewer GPUs and only a few million dollars.

Open-source models like Bonsai (27 billion parameters, 5.9GB) can run locally on MacBooks or Windows, prompting debate over why frontier closed-source models can continue charging premium pricing as open-source capabilities approach 98% of frontier levels on benchmarks.

Integrating models with software, tools, and execution systems reveals significant cost and quality gaps between open-source and frontier models, likely dividing the market between cheap models for routine tasks and premium models for complex tasks.

Although Vercel data shows open-source API share expanded from 20% to 80% while closed-source fell to 20%, top frontier models still generate massive revenue because enterprise customers pay high token prices for mission-critical tasks.

Commercial competition forces firms to use top-tier models for critical research despite spending 10 to 30 times more, but businesses face margin compression because they cannot easily pass higher AI software costs on to customers.

Leading frontier AI labs must continuously spend heavily on computing power to maintain their advantage, as seen in Anthropic pacing compute purchases weekly while OpenAI aggressively procured massive capacity.

Leading AI foundation model developers face a strategic trade-off between spending massive capital to acquire compute power and managing costs to remain competitive, as demonstrated by the divergent compute-purchasing strategies of Anthropic and OpenAI.
David Sacks argues that Anthropic's push for heightened AI safety regulation is an attempt at regulatory capture to slow down competitors while Anthropic deals with its own compute constraints.

The All-in podcast anticipates that Anthropic's IPO will face valuation pressure due to open-source competition, concentrated customer revenue, massive capital requirements, and management's contradictory public messaging regarding existential risks.

Anthropic's IPO has been delayed, and if its IPO is poorly priced or its post-IPO shares experience a sharp decline, it could negatively impact the entire AI industry, including hardware suppliers like Nvidia and Micron.

All-in podcast hosts debated Anthropic's leadership, with Jason advocating for replacing CEO Dario Amodei due to his controversial public statements, while Chamath opposed removing him because Amodei established the company's unique culture.

Chamath argues that Dario Amodei created a unique culture at Anthropic enabling it to transition from a follower to successfully challenging OpenAI, making it highly competitive in attracting top talent against firms like 8090 due to high growth and strong compensation.

calls.thesis: Maintain a long-term bullish stance on AI stocks such as Nvidia despite potential short-term volatility or delays in Anthropic's IPO, because long-term demand for compute far outstrips supply.
risks: Anthropic IPO delay or post-IPO price slump negatively impacting broader AI sentiment and hardware suppliers in the short term

calls.thesis: Closely monitor developments around Anthropic, as potential regulatory safety scares or issues surrounding its IPO could create headwinds for the AI sector and related suppliers.
conditions: if public alarm over AI regulation or safety issues intensifies around the IPO
risks: IPO pricing pressure and subsequent equity weakness impacting industry sentiment

sentences: The speaker notes that historical market panic around DeepSeek previously caused Nvidia's stock to decline from approximately $130 or $150 to around $80 on fears that top-tier models required fewer GPUs and only millions of dollars to train.

Discussion from the All-in podcast highlighted the Bonsai open-source model featuring 27 billion parameters and a 5.9GB footprint, which David Friedberg noted achieves 98 percent of frontier model capability while deploying locally on PCs.

Chamath Palihapitiya argued that when models are combined with operational execution systems and tools, product quality and cost diverge significantly from raw benchmark parity, segmenting the market into cheap models for routine workflows and frontier models for complex tasks.
Vercel platform data shared on the podcast indicated that open-source API call share expanded from 20 percent to 80 percent while closed-source API calls dropped from 80 percent to 20 percent.
David Sacks countered that despite the volume shift, top frontier labs still generate substantial revenue because enterprise clients willingly pay high token prices for mission-critical applications.

Frontier labs face significant capital trade-offs to maintain their competitive edge, with Anthropic's CFO historically evaluating compute purchases in weekly meetings while OpenAI pursued aggressive, unconstrained compute acquisition.

David Sacks argued that Anthropic's aggressive advocacy for government AI safety regulations amounts to regulatory capture designed to slow competitors while it manages internal compute capacity constraints.

The All-in podcast projected that Anthropic's upcoming IPO will face price down-rounds from investors due to customer concentration, huge ongoing capital needs, open-source competition, and conflicting public messaging regarding a 10 percent risk of human extinction.

The discussion noted that Anthropic's IPO has been delayed, and warned that a poor IPO price or steep post-listing drop could negatively depress market sentiment across the AI sector, directly impacting suppliers like Nvidia and Micron.

Podcast host Jason Calacanis advocated for replacing CEO Dario Amodei due to controversial public statements, but Chamath opposed this, noting Amodei successfully built a culture capable of challenging OpenAI and consistently winning top industry talent from firms like 8090.

Despite short-term volatility or delays surrounding Anthropic's IPO, the speaker maintains a long-term bullish stance on AI leaders like Nvidia because structural demand for compute continues to far exceed supply.
